title: The Divine Logos and Creation
english: Regarding the one saying through the Holy Spirit, 'and they shall worship you, and in you they shall pray; for in you is God, and there is no other besides you. For you are God' (Rev 22:8), you see how he uproots the skillful cunning of those teaching falsely. Likewise, there the prophet discourses about the Word having taken our flesh. A spirit of shadow could never have become a creative spirit. And because he is God himself, the Savior said, 'Spirit, God' (John 1:1). And because God is light, he himself teaches us, saying, 'I am the light' (John 8:12).

For who else, whether of the holy angels or of righteous men, was reliable enough to loose the penalty set for him from the face of God, if not the Word himself, who is both co-existing and co-forming, toward whom the Father said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Gen 1:26), with no other god existing who would be able to co-form with him? 'I am,' he says, 'the first God, and I after these things, and besides me no other god exists.' Nor was there any younger god, nor was any other god being 'after these things' able to work together with God.

But if anyone uses a small and human example like ours to examine the divine action as if through an icon: just as a skilled man who is a statue-maker, desiring to fashion a man, first observes his forms and characters within himself, then conceives what breadth and length is becoming, and examines the proportion of the whole in each individual part, having prepared the appropriate material of bronze, and having modeled the coming man after his own intellect and seeing him mentally, consciously cooperating with the Logos—by which he reasons and by which he is accustomed to do all things (for nothing beautiful comes into being without the Logos)—beginning this sensible work, he exhorts himself as if to another, saying, 'Come, let us make, come, let us fashion a man';

Thus the Lord of all, God, making the ensouled man from the earth, exhorts no one else but his own Logos, saying, 'Let us make man' (Gen 1:26), not in the same way as the others; for the whole creation came into being by the Logos. For God did not need any other preparation, such as matter or some other human thing, but this preparation which is in his own intellect.

Since it was impossible to conceive of God apart from the Word and the wisdom approaching the Word regarding the construction of the heavens, he rightly said, 'Whenever he was preparing the heavens, I was with him' (Proverbs 8:30). For before the world existed, the Word was in the Father. When the Almighty God set to make all things in the heavens and upon the earth, the genesis of the world required an active energy. And because of this, with no other existing besides God (for all is confessed to have come from him), the Word, having come forth, became the maker of the world, he who previously was inwardly preparing it, just as the prophet Solomon teaches us, saying, 'Whenever he was preparing the heavens, I was with him' (Proverbs 8:30) and 'As he was establishing springs under the heavens, whenever he was making the strong foundations of the earth, I was with him, fittingly joined to him; I was there as he was being applied' (Proverbs 8:29). For the Father rightly rejoiced in making all things through the Word with wisdom and power.

Just as all things that happened came from the Father through the Word, so also the things said by the Father are signified through the Word. For this reason also the most holy Moses names the Word an angel there, because he appeared through no other, but so that he might announce to Moses those things which he knew would be effective for the sons of Israel; and he knew they would be effective for believing that there is one God. Therefore also to him he said, 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14), in order that he might teach that no other besides himself is God. This is easy, I think, for those thinking well to know from a small and humble example among us. For it is not possible for anyone to separate the word of a man in power and substance; for the word is one and the same to a man, and is not separated from anything else, except by the energy of the act alone.

Here the Father says 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14) to Moses, but he says it clearly through the Word. For all that the Father says, he seems to be saying everywhere through the Word. And this is clear also from ourselves, in whatever small things we compare to the great and divine; for we also do all that we wish to say and do through our own word, according to our ability.

What then, does Asterios suppose the one saying 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14) to be, the Son or the Father? For two substances, setting aside the one which the Word of God took flesh into, the human one, and [...]

title: The Distinction of Hypostases
english: By imagining him thus, he calls the Father and the Son to be such, thereby separating the Son of God from the Father, just as anyone would separate a son of a man from his father according to nature. If he is said to have spoken these things to Moses while separating the Father from himself as the Son, he will not confess the Son to be God. For how can he allow the one saying 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14) not to agree that the Being says he is in opposition to non-being? But if he would posit the Son as being separated, he would be said to say 'I am the Being' regarding the Father as well. Either of these is impious.

Therefore, I shall begin to oppose each of those who have written incorrectly, starting from the epistle written by him. He wrote to believe in the Father as God the Almighty, and in his Son the only-begotten God, the Lord our Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit; and he says that he has learned this way of godliness from the divine writings. And I, when he says this, accept the things said very much, for this is the common way of godliness for all of us, to believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; but when, not having considered the divine, he says the Father is Father and the Son is Son more humanly to us through some technical theory, one can no longer praise such a theory as harmless. For through such a theory, the heresy currently conceived by them comes to increase, which I think is easy to demonstrate clearly from his own words. For he said that one must believe the Father to be truly Father and the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit likewise.

For it is impossible for three hypostases to be one unity, unless the Trinity first has its beginning from a unity. For the holy Paul said that those things are being recapitulated into a unity, which differ from God in nothing regarding unity; for the Word and the Spirit alone differ from God in unity.

If, therefore, the Word seems to have come forth from the Father and come to us, and the Holy Spirit, as Asterius also confessed, proceeds from the Father, the Savior immediately says concerning the Spirit that 'he will not speak of himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are coming' (John 16:13).

"He shall take from mine and he will announce to you" (John 16:5), the monad does not appear here clearly and manifestly, but in a secret word, expanding into a trinity yet by no means undergoing division. For if the Word proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit also is confessed to proceed from the Father, and immediately regarding the Spirit the Savior says, "He shall take from mine and he will announce to you" (John 16:5), is it not then evident that a mystery is being hidden to be revealed? For how, if the monad being undivided were not expanding into a trinity, could it contain him regarding the Spirit to say at times that he proceeds from the Father, and at times to say, "He shall take from mine and he will announce to you" (John 16:5), and immediately after having breathed upon the disciples, "Receive Holy Spirit" (John 20:22) having said?

For how, if he proceeds from the Father, does he promise to receive this ministry from the Son? For it is necessary either that, being divided into two, as Asterius said, there be persons, or that the Spirit proceeding from the Father must not be in need of the ministry from the Son (for everything proceeding from the Father must be perfect, by no means being dependent on the help of another), or, if he receives from the Son and by his power ministers the grace, he no longer proceeds from the Father. If, however, the Gospel said that having breathed upon the disciples, "Receive Holy Spirit" (John 20:22), he had said, it is evident that the Spirit came forth from the Word. How then, if the Spirit proceeded from the Word, does it again proceed from the Father?

Therefore, he has not spoken correctly nor appropriately, having said that there are three hypostases, not once, but a second time. We know the economy according to the flesh to differ for the man, but we have believed the incorcorporeality according to the spirit to be united to the Father. For if the examination of the Spirit were the only one, it would seem fitting that the Word be one and the same with God; but if the addition according to the flesh upon the Savior were being examined, it seems that the divinity is being expanded by energy alone, so that it would seem fitting that the monad truly is undivided.

For Asterius had decided that there are one and the same, according to this, only the Father and the Son, in accordance with which they agree in all things. For so he said: and because of the precise [account] in all words and works...

title: The Harmony of the Son and Father
english: Regarding the harmony of 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). If, therefore, He himself says these things: 'I went forth from the Father and I have come,' and again, 'and the Word, which you hear, is not mine, but belongs to Him who sent me the Father,' and 'all things that the Father has are mine' (John 16:15), it is clear that He was rightly saying even that: 'the Father is in me and I in the Father' (John 16:33), so that the Word, saying this, might be in God, and the Father might be in the Word, because the Word is the power of the Father. For a trustworthy witness has declared Him to be 'the power of God and the wisdom of God.'

The Savior does not say 'I and the Father are one' because of a precise harmony in all words and works, as Asterius said, but because it is impossible to divide the Word of God or God Himself from the Word. Since Asterius thinks the Savior said this because of a harmony in everything, and desires to learn the truth without paying attention to the second economy, it is necessary to remind him how, at times, one sees what appears to be a discord. For such is what the spoken words teach us.

For what kind of harmony is there in the time of the passion when He says this, 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me' (Luke 22:42), but then adds that, 'yet not as I will, but as You' (Luke 22:42)? For there was no harmony at first in saying, 'let this cup pass from me'; nor does it seem that there is any agreement in what is being added, for He says, 'not my will, but Yours, Father, let it be done.' You hear how the letter declares a discord, according to appearances, of the one willing and of the one not willing. For the Father clearly willed that which willed happened through the things from which it was clear; but the Son's not willing is made clear through the things by which He renounces it. And again He says, 'I do not seek my own will, but the will of Him who sent me the Father' (John 5:30). How, then, does he say that the Savior said, 'I and the Father are one' because of a harmony in everything?

How can the Son have harmony toward the Father, or the Father toward the Son, when the Son says, 'all things that the Father has are mine' (John 16:15)? For, contrary to the Son encroaching upon the Father, he says, 'all things that the Father has are mine.' For this reason, passing over the fact that all things the Father has are common, he said, 'all things that the Father has are mine.'

Even if it was not proper for the one in agreement to speak in this way, rather: all that the Father has is common. For if the Acts of the Apostles, praising the agreement of those approaching with faith like the ones mentioned, said, "all things were common to them" (Acts 4:32), and one ought to consider all things to be common for men capable of agreeing, how much more ought the Father and the Son to partake in communion, being divided into two hypostases?

But now, in saying, "all that the Father has is mine" (John 16:15), the Son seems to be grasping at the Father's; and in stating that not even his own word is master, but rather the Father of this [word] (for he says, "the word which you hear is not mine but of Him who sent me, the Father" [John 8:28]), it shows the Father being deprived of his own things of the Son. Furthermore, according to the opinion of Asterius, the two sides seem not to have spoken in accordance. For the one in agreement ought not to justly snatch away what belongs to the other, for this is grasping, but ought to consider what belongs to each to be common.

So when we look down toward the flesh in a human way, we will not find the Savior having said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), just as Asterius has written. For it was not because of the precise agreement in all words and works, as he himself has written, that the Savior said, "I and the Father are one." For if it were this, he certainly would have said: "I and the Father agree with one another in all things." But now he said, "I and the Father are one."

So if there were any disagreement in those [things], and since the Lord must speak the truth, it is fitting to know the Savior precisely, that whenever he says, "I and the Father are one," he says this not looking down toward the man whom he took upon himself, but toward the Word proceeding from the Father. For if any disagreement were thought to exist, this ought to be referred to the weakness of the flesh, which the Word did not have previously when he was taken. But if unity were being spoken of, this seems to differ from the Word. Therefore, not only did he say, "I and the Father are one" appropriately, but also that: "For such a long time I have been with you, Philip, and you say: show me the Father" (John 14:9), it is clear that [he said this] for those capable of seeing the intelligible things not with these eyes, but with the intellectual ones. For both the Father and his Word exist invisible to the eyes of the flesh. Therefore, not because of the agreement in all things...
